utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you. And then, as you may see from the Scheduling Order, in addition may I ask who appears for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as for my health, it is not too good, but I don't think I have any special problems. My blood pressure is being kept under control, that is. utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OBRENOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED OBRENOVIC

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED JOKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my health is excellent. Thank you for the confidence you have shown in granting me provisional release, and I have absolutely no complaints against the conditions in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand what is being said in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand what is being said in the courtroom. I have no complaints and no health problems. I have no complaints against the conditions in the Detention Unit either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have a long agenda today. Just to have the overview for you, the first issue to be addressed is the one of the conditions of provisional release; second, a number of questions related to disclosure; possibilities to proceed more expeditiously by use of 94 bis statements, by use of depositions under Rule 71; and other possibilities; first of all, the possibility to come to agreed facts. Before I start with the first point on the agenda, why all this speeding up at this point in time? The reason is that in all likelihood -- one never knows what happens in this Tribunal, but in all likelihood, the case we have before us will be heard as of May 6, 2003. Then a Trial Chamber will be ready, and the two necessary ad litem Judges will be assigned as soon as possible for this case. In the meantime, no doubt we will have either another Status Conference, as foreseen in the Rules, or a Pre-Trial Conference. And in preparation of today's Status Conference, we faced some problems that should be resolved before we are starting the case and before we are conferring another Status Conference or Pre-Trial Conference. That the issue before us can also be understood by the public, I'll just recall the events. On 28 March 2002, this Trial Chamber denied the request of the accused Jokic regarding his provisional release. This decision was invalidated by Appeals Chamber decision of 28 May 2002. Provisional release was granted. As far as we can see, the accused Jokic lived up to all the expectations and the obligations under this order. When we conferred this Status Conference, it was our intention to discuss the issue what shall happen when a case starts for trial and a person is provisionally released, and it was foreseen to discuss this issue under the headline "Proportionality, necessity," because in some jurisdictions it is the rule - I don't want to discuss human rights at this point in time - it is the rule that once provisionally released, it is not mandatory that, when starting a trial, the accused has to come back to the Detention Unit. This would be settled today. When inviting for the Status Conference and asking Mr. Jokic to appear in the Detention Unit, we were confronted with a motion to modify the conditions of appearance for the Status Conference, filed on 15 November 2002. Taking into account the principle of proportionality, first of all, this means that a measure in criminal law and in international law is proportional only when, first, suitable; second, necessary; and three, its degree and scope remain in reasonable relationship to the envisaged target. That's proportionality in its narrowest sense. And taking into account that procedural measures should be never capricious or excessive and it is sufficient to use a more lenient measure, when this is the case, this measure must be applied. Therefore, we granted leave and allowed the accused Jokic not to go to the Detention Unit but to take care himself on his own accommodation during this Status Conference. In response, the Government of the Netherlands disagreed, and they made reference to an earlier statement of - let me see. Where is it? - January 28. There it reads: "It is the understanding of the Netherlands that upon his provisional release, Mr. Jokic will leave Dutch territory." And consequently, on November 22, 2002, we got the information that: "In the view of the Netherlands authorities, Mr. Jokic staying outside of the United Nations Detention Unit would be contrary to this condition. The Netherlands therefore cannot agree to Mr. Jokic's stay in a hotel during his stay in the Netherlands, but is of course prepared to provide its usual assistance in transferring ICTY accused to the United Nations Detention Unit." We want to express the gratitude in the direction of Defence counsel and Mr. Jokic that he voluntarily decided under these circumstances to go to the Detention Unit, which in fact made it unnecessary to come to a ruling balancing the interests of the Netherlands on the one side and human rights on the other side. Knowing that there is this problem and there will be this problem in the future as well, it is necessary to discuss this issue. And may I first invite Defence counsel to discuss and submit their point of view in a two-fold approach. I think it's a different question whether an accused when returning for the purposes of a Status Conference or Pre-Trial Conference or when he's reappearing for trial. So may I please hear your submissions. What is your point of view to this first factual and, second, legal issue? Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when preparing for today's Status Conference, and after we received the Scheduling Order for today's Status Conference, as the Defence team, we had several talks among ourselves and with our defendant, Mr. Jokic. On this occasion, I wish to state that, first of all, we would like to thank the Chamber for its understanding in respect of the status of Dragan Jokic under Rule 65 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We have not had any doubts for a single moment as to whether we would fulfil all the obligations stemming from the Scheduling Order for today's conference. Dragan Jokic is fulfilling in every detail all the decisions passed by the Trial Chamber, both in respect of his own behaviour, the safety of others, and as regards his personal security. We assure you that throughout his provisional release, he will continue to fulfil all the obligations stemming from the Trial Chamber's decision. We also assure you that he will respect all decisions of the Trial Chamber regarding his return to the Detention Unit when the Chamber deems it necessary. When preparing for the Status Conference, yesterday we were informed that in late March or early April another Status Conference is expected which may be joined to a Pre-Trial Conference, bearing in mind the date that has been set for the beginning of this trial. We wish to take this opportunity to ask the Trial Chamber, if there is no special need for the arrival of the accused Dragan Jokic to the next Status Conference or Pre-Trial Conference, that we not bring him here again on that occasion because this leads to great expenses, a lot of work, and the recruitment of seven to eight people who took part in the execution of this obligation. We also wish to ask, respecting, of course, the views of the Trial Chamber should they be opposed to this, that before his -- that the period of the accused's arrival before the start of the trial be less than 60 days, taking into account all the reasons and all the elements required when determining his detention. So we apply that he be allowed to come to the Detention Unit a brief period before the beginning of his trial. Further, in our talks with our defendant, Mr. Jokic, last night, we discussed the possibility of raising our submissions as to whether it is necessary for Jokic to be in the Detention Unit during the time of the trial. We agreed that we should inform Your Honours that, respecting all our obligations, we shall organise ourselves in such a manner that Dragan Jokic will stay at the Detention Unit during the trial. Dragan Jokic and we as our Defence team have reached this decision in view of the fact the conditions exist for him to continue communicating with his Defence team in the Detention Unit to prepare for his defence, that his personal security will be better if he is in the Detention Unit, and bearing in mind that, according to the Trial Chamber's decision, he must bear the expenses of his arrival and departure and any stay outside the Detention Unit, and since these expenses are quite onerous for the accused Dragan Jokic, and also bearing in mind what Your Honours have stated in item 2, bearing all this in mind, we wish to say that during the trial, Dragan Jokic will stay in the Detention Unit and not outside the Detention Unit. And objectively, we realise that it may not even be possible for him not to be in the Detention Unit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you very much for your submission which makes more clear what is the issue before us. It seems to be limited now to the question whether or not an accused has, when reappearing for the purposes of a Status Conference or Pre-Trial Conference or another initial hearing or whatever may -- whenever it may be necessary, that an accused appears for, say, one or two days in the Netherlands, being provisionally released, whether in these cases it is mandatory de facto, whereas it seems to be de jure not necessary and it might be even an infringement of the principle of proportionality. Therefore, we only have to discuss this latter question, because in the case before us, apparently we do not have the problem of a request for modifying the order as to the fact as it was done by the Defence in this case to allow the accused to stay in another accommodation. So may I ask the Prosecution, what is your opinion on this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, as you're aware, the Prosecution took no position on the issue of the day or two stay during this particular Status Conference. As for a future Status Conference, the position of the Prosecution is largely -- would largely be the same, though I would like to hear from the Dutch government and from the Registry on their point of view. From the practical point of view and from the position of proportionality, a day or two of freedom during a Status Conference does not present any problem for the Prosecution, though I would like to retain the right to change that position after hearing from the Registry and from the Dutch government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the Dutch government not regard this as an act of non-courtesy when I first ask the Registry to comment on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROHDE
utterances.text: Your Honours, my comments will be very brief only. As the Trial Chamber is aware, we are providing accommodation for accused at a very high standard. This is always available. The conditions are excellent. This pertains particularly to safety for the accused, medical attention, psychiatric attention if needed, other professional care, and things like that. So from that viewpoint, the Registry is offering, we believe, excellent conditions and has, I think, no further comments on another arrangement as proposed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally, in fact, it seems limited to an exchange of different views, especially taken by the government of the Netherlands, and I know that it was more or less by surprise that they were asked to decide on this critical question. I'm aware of this, but as it is always in the -- in criminal procedure, you can't foresee what will happen. We tried to foresee and do the necessary in relation to the trial and to avoid the discussion immediately before we start the trial, but now we have the same problem in a nutshell related to this one or two days stay in the Netherlands. So may I ask you, Mr. Lammers, or one of your colleagues, in order for a better understanding. It may be more appropriate for you to come Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here and to give us your submission, please. And I want to emphasise that the representatives of the Dutch government appear today in their capacity as friends of the Court, amici curiae.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for the invitation to attend this Status Conference concerning for Mr. Jokic. We agree that the invitation came rather late. Actually, we had only one day to prepare ourselves for this meeting, and so it was not very easy, and actually, very principal questions are involved. We have been asked to present our opinion as host country in the capacity of an amicus curiae on the question whether it is necessary or even mandatory for the accused to be detained in the UN Detention Unit during pre-trial or during the trial phase. I now understand that the issue is no longer whether the accused should stay or not within the UN Detention Unit in the Netherlands during the trial period. So as you said, we should limit ourselves to the question of whether he should stay in the UN Detention Unit during pre-trial session or during a conference, a Status Conference. You may recall that the Netherlands has sent the Court a -- the Tribunal a letter, actually, the day after the decision was taken by the Trial Chamber that Mr. Jokic should be allowed to stay in a hotel in The Hague under certain conditions. Actually, we deplore that this decision has been taken by the Trial Chamber without first consulting the Netherlands government on this matter. As we understand Rule 65(B) of the Rules of the Tribunal, the Netherlands should be consulted before, not only on the question whether provisional release should be granted, but also on the conditions under which this provisional release should be granted, and it is our understanding that if conditions are to be changed on this point, that the Netherlands should be consulted first. Anyway, the Netherlands has expressed its objections against the stay of Mr. Jokic outside the UN Detention Unit also in respect of a Status Conference, on the occasion of a Status Conference or on the occasion of a pre-trial meeting, because the Netherlands has special obligations concerning protecting Mr. Jokic, safeguarding his safety, and so on, and this is a considerable burden on the Netherlands authorities. This would, of course, be a major case when the accused should stay outside -- should stay in the Netherlands, outside the UN Detention Unit, during the trial period. But fortunately, this situation is not to be discussed at this moment. It still remains so that we maintain, actually, our objections against the stay of Mr. Jokic outside the UN Detention Unit in the Netherlands, also for the shorter periods. In exceptional cases, we have allowed an accused in the past to stay in a hotel, but that was only because the time period between the release from the Detention Unit and the flight was such that the accused should stay in a hotel. But that was only in an exceptional situation, and we would not consider that to be the normal case. So we should also consider this from the point of view of the safety of Mr. Jokic. As already said by the Registrar, the safety of Mr. Jokic is better assured when he is in the UN Detention Unit than when he is outside the UN Detention Unit in the Netherlands; and this is a very important reason, I think, to keep in mind. We also understand that from the part of Mr. Jokic himself, practical and financial reasons, he actually prefers to stay in the UN Detention Unit, and it seems that when we take all these aspects together - the point of view of the Public Prosecutor, the point of view expressed by the Registrar, the point of view expressed by the counsel for Mr. Jokic, and the objections raised by the Netherlands, and taking into account also the fact that, according to my information, human rights convention would not be opposed against a person who has been provisionally released to be detained during his trial or during other meetings with the Tribunal in a detention unit - so for all these reasons, I think the Netherlands should maintain its objections. Well, that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I first clarify two issues. First, Rule 65(B) provides, no doubt, that the host country, given an opportunity to provide its opinion when the question of provisional release, as such, granting provisional release, is at stake, and no doubt in this case this opportunity was given and the Netherlands agreed that there would be provisional release but, as mentioned, under the condition an accused leaves immediately the country when on provisional release. We have to make a differentiation between two kinds of deprivation of liberty. There's, on the one hand, the deprivation of liberty for the purpose of safeguarding the procedure against a person presumed innocent; and on the other hand, a deprivation of liberty for purposes of his or her own safety. These two issues should never be confused. So finally, the point is that under the current circumstances -- and I discuss this issue in detail, for the reason that it's not the only case where we will face this problem in the future. It might be that also, among others, one may be provisionally released by an Appeals Chamber, we could have the same problem. And we heard by the Defence counsel no doubt that he would ask that Mr. Jokic should be requested to come to the Netherlands for the purposes of such short conferences only when it's mandatory and absolutely necessary. But under the Rules, in certain occasions, it's mandatory and it is necessary that an accused appears. So we can't foresee this. And I think we have to -- not to resolve it today, but we have to hear exhaustive submissions by the parties and, also in this case, by the Netherlands, being involved and no doubt part of these proceedings. The question comes down to the core question: Under the host country agreement, we have the provision allowing for bringing a person to and from the Detention Unit, Schiphol airport, and another airport in the Netherlands. But apparently the mothers and fathers of our Statute and our Rules did not foresee at that time that there would be any provisional release, and now we are facing the situation that we have only two possibilities: either a person being in the Detention Unit or in his or her home country. It would not be possible to have this person for one or two days in the Netherlands without being in the Detention Unit. I may recall that nearly all European laws on criminal procedure provide for provisional release, and as far as I know, in the Netherlands it's the case that, when once decided that it is not necessary to have a person in detention in the Detention Unit, then he or she may appear as an ordinary citizen, presumed innocent, to trial; and only when there are new facts, there is a possibility for the Chamber to reconsider their previous decision and to come to other conclusions. But de facto, in the moment, it would not be possible for accused in this Tribunal and, I add, also other tribunals in the future, criminal tribunals in the future, to grant provisional release and allowing these persons to stay in the Netherlands, which no doubt in some circumstances - and this broadens a little bit the scope of the issue before us - which no doubt allows the Trial Chambers more easily to come to the conclusion that provisional release may be granted. So may I ask you once again, taking into account these other legal systems and principles, predominantly applied in Europe, whether or not it is the position of the Dutch government not to allow provisional release for the purpose of one or two days, or even in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, indeed, I think we should make a distinction between a situation where there is a request for a provisional release of a person, and then the question will arise whether he will or will not pose a danger to any victim witness or other person, so for a third person, so to say, on the one hand; and the situation that a person may not pose such a danger to third persons but that he himself may be the object of danger. It is in respect of the latter situation that I would like to say the following: It may be so that also according to Netherlands criminal procedural law, a person may not be detained in a detention unit when he has been provisionally released, but I think that here we have a different situation in the sense that the question arises: Who is to be responsible for the safety and the guarantee of the safety of Mr. Jokic when he is outside the -- when he is in the Netherlands and outside the UN Detention Unit? And this is a special burden on the Netherlands government, and we still believe that this burden should be limited as much as possible. And so that is the reason that, in principle, we feel ourselves obliged, of course, to provide this service of safeguarding a person when he comes from abroad and goes to the Tribunal or the UN Detention Unit, or from there back to his country. But the burden on the Netherlands outside that should remain as limited as possible. And I think the situation is different here in the sense that this is a procedure before an international tribunal; and in the case of the Netherlands, when a person is prosecuted before a Dutch court and the court decides that he may be provisionally released, then it's a matter entirely within the legal -- the Dutch legal system. So for that reason, I think that the situation is not entirely comparable with the situation before a national judicial instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand that you have to represent the interest, also taking into account security aspects, but nevertheless, is it really true that a distinction can be made between, on the one hand side, an accused prosecuted in a Dutch court and, on the other hand, a person, a human being presumed innocent - this has to be emphasised - and prosecuted by an international criminal tribunal? Isn't it something a host country has to take into account when inviting an international tribunal to the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the situation is not, to my belief, with all due respect, entirely identical with a case entirely before a Dutch court, and I think that a balance in this case has to be made between the interests of the accused, the interests of the Tribunal, and the interests of the Dutch government. And when I take into consideration the fact that there is a special responsibility on the Netherlands in respect of this type of accused persons, to safeguard their safety, to protect their person, and I don't have the figures of the cost involved apart from the political and administrative burden of the cost involved for one day in a hotel, but we computed the costs of an annual safety provision on around-the-clock basis for one person, and we came to the conclusion that this would cost somewhere between 600.000 euro and 1 million euro on an annual basis. So maybe this gives an indication of what the costs, apart from the political and administrative and the technical problems, would be -- would be in the case of the special precautionary measures which the Netherlands government would have to take. If we set this in respect, on the one hand, and take into consideration, on the other hand, the good accommodation in the UN Detention Unit and also the fact that his safety may be more -- may be more protected in the UN Detention Unit, it does not seem to me self-evident that the accused should be in a Dutch hotel. I would also like to emphasise that in spite of -- to indicate the burden which is on the host state, not only on the host state but also on the state where the accused goes to, that I only have to refer to the guarantees which the Republika Srpska government was asked to give in the case of the provisional release of Mr. Jokic. The government of -- the Republika Srpska government had to guarantee that it would organise security for Mr. Jokic and ensure that he does not leave his place of residence without approval and that if he is not complying with the conditions of his provisional release, that they should arrest him, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. So it indicates that there is a rather special burden on the part of the government in the Netherlands when the person is not within the UN Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is not our intention to decide immediately on this issue, and it is to be discussed in the framework of a Bureau meeting, without any doubt, because it's a matter of principle and a harmonised approach by our Trial Chamber is needed. But may I ask the parties: Are there any additional remaining questions related to this issue and this, as a matter of principle, this can be the case and can be the problem in the future for other accused in this case? Does anybody want to raise a question or to submit an opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might also just remind the Court that the Pre-Trial Conference that is coming up, we will be requesting the same modification of conditions as set by the Court. So the issue dealing with temporary provisional release of the accused is still very much alive, although we have stated that he will submit to the UN Detention Unit during trial. If he's ordered back during the Pre-Trial Conference, then we would request the same conditions of modification. We also apologise to the Dutch government and to the Trial Chamber for the untimeliness of the motion that we filed, and I'm hoping that if this other motion and request is filed in a more timely manner, that the Dutch government will have more time to consider this, and once they see that there are no security issues concerning Mr. Jokic and that the Court ordered that the Defence be responsible for his safety and security, that possibly they would take a different position on this. But there's still the issue now of weighing the interest -- human rights interest, and the presumption of innocence with Mr. Jokic, who, I'm not sure what the Dutch government meant when they said "this type of accused person" versus another type of accused person with the interest of the Dutch government. And we still submit that this issue is alive, and we will be submitting another request during the Pre-Trial Conference. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other Defence counsel wanting to take the floor? I can't see. The Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have nothing to say at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It remains for me to thank you very much for coming today. I think it's worthwhile reconsidering this question, especially related to the issue we have before us, the upcoming Pre-Trial Conference, where it may be necessary for one or other reasons to address the accused in person and to grant him the possibility to be. We also have to take this into account. The accused is not the object. He's a subject, the main person of such a case, and no doubt he has the right to attend a hearing when his future is discussed and the charges against him and how to proceed, especially during a Pre-Trial Conference. Then he has the right to be here. So taking into account that it was indeed on a very short notice, I would invite the Dutch government to present their final opinion in writing, if it's possible. I don't want to impose any time limit on the government, but hopefully before the winter court recess of this Tribunal. This is the 13th of December. If this would be possible, we would be extremely grateful that we can know what is the basis on what we have to decide in future. Thank you very much for coming. And when closing this point on the agenda, we take the opportunity of having a break now until 10.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAMMERS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, it should be mentioned that we continue now in the absence of the representative of the Dutch government and the representative of the Registry, and we continue with the Pre-Trial Judge only, we having before us now ordinary, practical issues. And let us start immediately media in res, and let's discuss issues of disclosure. As regards 66(A)(i), I think there is no longer any problem. The disclosure under this paragraph is complete. What about 66(A)(ii)? Are there any complaints we cannot find in the motions? I'm aware that we have a number of motions before us still pending, but I would appreciate if we could resolve these problems during the Status Conference. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Who wants to take the floor first from the Defence? Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I take it this is an invitation, Your Honour -- thank you, first of all. I take it this is an invitation to discuss, in general, the issue of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's -- it would be appropriate first to limit it to 66 issues, and then later on to 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Great. Because I think, in my opinion, Your Honour, perhaps the crux of the problem, at least from our position, is that everything emanates from Rule 66. As I've indicated in the past, it's my firm belief, given that the Prosecution has drafted a very broad indictment, given that they have charged Mr. Blagojevic, in essence, from the beginning, in this joint criminal enterprise, that we should be entitled to have the entire file on Srebrenica from the Prosecution, with the exception of any material which they may feel comes under work product. And of course, they do have the opportunity, if they feel that certain material should not be revealed to the Defence, they can seek guidance from the Court to see whether that material should not be revealed to the Defence. So we do have a motion. The motion is still pending. I understand the Prosecution's position. Yesterday they indicated - and I'm sure Mr. McCloskey will correct me if I misstate anything - that they will comply with their obligations to provide material which they believe is material to the Defence. And I think that's the critical aspect of this, because, I dare say, I certainly do not want the Prosecutor telling me what he believes is material to the Defence, because I believe the entire file is material. The real issue is: Do statements come under the ambit of disclosed material as far as documents are concerned? And we suggest, and we urge the Court, that the answer to that is yes. And why is that? In the past, this Rule, as I understand it, has somewhat narrowly been viewed, perhaps not challenged as well. I know they have challenged it in Arusha. But a statement on its face may not appear to be material, but given to the Defence, and with investigation - because this is an adversarial process - it may lead to other material evidence, other material witnesses. And therefore, we contend, because of the nature of the indictment, which the Prosecution drafted and which the Court has indicated should stand as is, and upon which we must defend, that we should be entitled to everything. The Prosecution indicated that they would provide us with all -- they said they will provide statements. I didn't hear "all statements contained in all of their files." That's what I would like to hear. I don't know if Mr. McCloskey is in a position to make that sort of announcement here today. Perhaps he has to run it up the ladder. Perhaps he doesn't wish to set a precedent in this particular case. And that's why we may need your assistance in ruling on the motion. But that is our position as far as disclosure material. Aside from that particular issue, we are getting statements from the Prosecution that were obtained back in 2000 or 2001. We're just getting them now because they haven't been translated. Mr. Blagojevic indicated to me that I should have my translator, or translators, working on translating all of these statements because he needs to see them. Well, obviously, one, that's impossible because we don't have those resources; secondly, it's not our obligation; and thirdly, the question must be asked: Why is it taking so long? Especially when the Prosecution has come in and said, "Well, the indictment was outstanding since 1998." Obviously they were waiting to pick him up. So now here we are 2002, getting close to 2003, and we're just getting these statements. I'm not saying that Mr. McCloskey is holding back on the translations. They have some technical problems. But it is affecting our ability to, one, prepare our case, because without these statements we cannot do a proper investigation. Obviously, the accused are entitled to see them. And that is holding up -- that's holding up the process, as far as I'm concerned. And I know that Mr. McCloskey is doing everything he possibly can, but I think we may need some reassurances from you, Your Honour, that something can be done to expedite this process. Because it does cause tension within the Defence teams, between the lawyer and the client, because the client wants the material. You know, I can't consult with the client on statements if he doesn't have it. Now, we've gone through the -- we've asked the Prosecutor, and they have been helpful in providing us tapes of interviews. Of course, it's very time-consuming for the accused to listen to all of the tapes and then prepare to go over statements in that fashion, but we're going to need those anyway for the trial. So basically, those are my opening remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before giving the floor to other Defence counsel, I want to emphasise that no doubt we have 66 before us, but as to the incredible amount of documents available, in principle, which might tend to have a connection to the case before us, it seems to be impossible to request all statements. From the point of view of the Chamber, the test should be: Might a document be relevant for the case? Relevance should be the appropriate test. And I understand fully your concern, coming from a civil law system where we have all the documents in one file and all the documents are accessible to all the parties and, first of all, also the Judges. It's also the Judges' concern that sometimes we really cannot decide on the relevance, for example, of a question put to a witness whether or not to admit evidence when we don't know the entire -- all the, I emphasise, relevant statements. I think when we discuss this issue, we should bear in mind that no doubt our Rules are primarily those ones emanating from a common law system. But nevertheless, common law and civil law, they have both one root, and to a certain extent this is the Roman rule and the Roman principle da mihi factum, dabo tibi jus; "Give me the facts, and I give you the law." This is for the Judges. And we also feel sometimes uncomfortable, but we have to understand that we have to work under Rule 66 in this case, and these Rules -- this Rule provides only for the mandatory disclosure of relevant material. And I hope that we can agree that relevance could be or should be the test applicable. As regards 66, 68, there, I think, another approach is necessary. But let us hear, in the order, the Defence of Mr. Obrenovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: May it please the Court. Your Honour, I endorse Mr. Karnavas's arguments this morning. I also endorse his concern which has nothing personally to do with Mr. McCloskey. We do not distrust Mr. McCloskey. If Mr. McCloskey and I suddenly changed seats, I believe that you would probably hear the same argument from him. There is a difficulty with the opposing party determining what is relevant for your case. This is an issue, and I do not know how it goes away. I also believe, based on the history of the litigation on this point, that Your Honour should rule on the outstanding motions and should announce some guidelines and some standards from which we will all be operating. Otherwise, I see this as something that will continue to plague us and continue to cause issues to be raised in Status Conferences and at 65 ter conferences. So the question was raised yesterday as to whether this is something that the parties can sit down and come to agreement to without your interference. Respectfully, I would think that it is not, and I believe that it is something that Your Honour should address and should provide us with the guidance and rule from the Court, and we will live by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. On behalf of Mr. Jokic, please. I think there we have a huge number of open issues in your motions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I may address the Court. There have been several motions for disclosure filed on behalf of Mr. Jokic, starting from April 15th and the most recent one filed this last week dealing with Rule 68, but the Court has asked that we address Rule 66 first, I believe. Under 66, our main concern is Rule 66(B). In our last motion we filed, we stand 100 per cent behind the ruling in Rutaganda, which holds that everything, all statements, fit under the ambit of discoverable material in -- under Rule 66(B). And the Court clarified that by stating that written statements by the accused should be considered as being included within the scope of documents to be disclosed by the Prosecutor to the Defence, as provided under Rule 66(B). Of course, the decision on -- the Court has mentioned "relevant," what is relevant evidence for the defence at this time. But Rule 66(B) states: "... evidence that is material to the preparation of the defence." So whether it is considered relevant by the Prosecutor as far as their theory of the case is something different than what we consider might be material evidence leading to relevant evidence in the Defence case. So it is a much broader scope under Rutaganda and a much broader scope under Rule 66(B). Instead of relevance, it's material, whether it's material to the preparation of the defence. I would also like to say that the Defence of Dragan Jokic joins in Mr. -- the arguments by Mr. Karnavas on behalf of Mr. Blagojevic that we don't have the funds, the wherewithal, or the staff to have all these translations done. We talked to the Prosecution yesterday and Mr. von Hebel about how we're going to solve these problems, and until we get full disclosure in the languages that we can communicate with our client with and we can all discuss the issues of the case, we can't really be prepared for a pre-trial brief until all of this is completed first. The motion filed on July 18th regarding disclosure by Mr. Jokic was withdrawn, so I'm putting it aside. And at this point, Dragan Jokic only asks that you rule on the April 15th motion and the September -- yes, the September 15th motion which are pending on disclosure regarding Rule 66, 66(A), 66(B), and 67, and we'll address Rule 68 after the Court decides on whether it will rule on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we agree that the question whether a document is material does not exclude to apply also the second attribute that is relevant, knowing very well that it is extremely difficult for both parties to label the documents 66 material, relevant; 68, exculpatory. And I, having served myself as Defence counsel for five years, I would be hesitant to leave it for the Prosecution to decide, for example, on the Rule 68, to label the document as exculpatory. It is for the Defence to decide whether they regard it as exculpatory. But let's stay with 66. I thank you for this clarification on the outstanding motions, and no doubt the Trial Chamber has to rule on this, but let us finally hear the observations by the Defence counsel for Mr. Nikolic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on behalf of Mr. Nikolic, it is our position that the Defence also has to have all the essential and relevant statements and all the materials which may be necessary to prepare for the defence. According to our opinion, the disclosure under 66(ii) -- (A)(i) has not been completed with regard to the accused Nikolic. We have not received all the witness statements, either in English or in B/C/S, that is, of all the witnesses which the Prosecution intends to call. We have got the list of witnesses. I have compared it with the statements, and I have established that we still lack a number of statements. We sincerely hope that this problem will soon be resolved with the OTP. And as far as the 66(B) is concerned, I believe that the Trial Chamber should decide. And I support my learned colleagues, and I don't want to waste any more time on that. I also support the position that the statements have to be relevant. I would like to give you an example. We have received a statement from the Prosecution which may not be relevant in this case. I am not going to say the full name of the witness because that witness may be protected, but her statement is relative to the year 1992, has nothing whatsoever to do with the year 1995, and I believe that this statement is not relevant for this case in which we are dealing with July through December 1995, as per the indictment. And I don't see the reason why the Prosecution has sent us this statement except to prejudice our client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this intervention. It shows in a nutshell the problem we all have to face here with this incredible number of documents. There are always complaints, being overwhelmed with a deluge of documents on one hand side, and on the other side the request for full compliance and giving access to all the documents available. But may we hear the submission and the view taken by the Prosecution to this question. And it's principally touching upon the question of translation, because here I believe it's a priority for the Trial Chamber to rule as soon as possible and to order that the -- I hesitate to say "the documents," but the important documents that the Defence needs, no doubt, for the preparation of their brief and their own investigations, that these parts are translated within due time. And what would be from your point of view a reasonable time for translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm a little surprised that -- about this argument. My records show that I have three witnesses who we interviewed in the last few weeks that we haven't been able to get full statements and translations of, but the indications I have is that almost all, if not all, the other witnesses that we intend to call under 66(ii) have been provided in both languages, and this is the first I've heard from counsel on this point, and we have a good working relationship. Mr. Veselin Londrovic is very good at pointing things out to us when we've missed it, and I'm sure he will continue to do that. And if there are items that he hasn't received, we will get them to him and the others as soon as possible. But I don't believe for -- in the purposes of the witnesses, that we have a problem with translations. We made huge efforts to get special translation services and special transcription services in place outside this country so that we would be able to have this material ready for the filing of the trial brief, and I believe we have met that in almost all cases. And if we have not, we will certainly make efforts to do so. And we shouldn't, you know, need much time at all to clear this problem up because I don't believe it exists in terms of 66(ii). And I'm always willing to hear their -- to speak with them and find out why they haven't received things, but they've been getting stuff, a lot of stuff. And it's not always easy to figure out everything you have, and I think that may be the problem more than lack of translations at this time, but I'll work with them to identify if there is truly a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And let's stay for a moment with the problem of translation. I heard that the pre-trial brief has not yet been translated into B/C/S. No doubt the accused has a right to have access to this pre-trial brief in a language he understands, and therefore my question is: Do you know anything about the development related to the translation of the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Most counsel and I have spoken about this, and we all agree as a practical reality that you're correct, the Defence should have this. The Rules, unfortunately, do not require it, so that faces -- we face a difficult problem. And I think you could assist us on that, and if we all jointly ask translations to do that, I would expect that it would be done in a relatively short time. But it's not something that's always done, and -- but counsel has indicated a great interest in this product and we would support them in that it should be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To conclude this, I think it is necessary and it will be done right now. Having discussed this issue with my colleagues, the -- we order that the pre-trial brief be translated in full no later than 10 December 2002. And from this it follows that we can't expect the Defence to prepare their pre-trial brief as scheduled - it was also the 10th of December - and anticipating all that what I heard from the 65 ter conference of yesterday, I think it's appropriate that we can expect the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Defence pre-trial brief 10 January 2003. Is this an adequate point in time? Mr. Morrison, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a great help to us, and this is what we were all hoping we would hear this morning. There is another aspect which bears very definitely on our ability to prepare our pre-trial brief, and that is the translation of the Butler report. It's a similar situation to the Prosecution's trial brief. This is a very technical document that Mr. Butler has prepared. It's again about the same size as the trial brief, many footnotes, et cetera. It is in many senses a very technical manual. It's very similar to that. Mr. McCloskey yesterday indicated that their own witness, who is a British general, who has been identified, has to have an opportunity to review Mr. Butler's report, and after he's had a chance to, as I recall the words, review and digest it, then he himself will be able to prepare a report. And as I understood Mr. McCloskey, he can't do that for a couple of months. I am not a professional soldier. I find it a very complex document. I do my best to understand it, but I need the help of Mr. Obrenovic, my client, to do that. All of these gentlemen are soldiers. It has great meaning to them, and for them to understand exactly what the nature of the case against them is, they really need to have an opportunity to review that, study it, tell us what they believe is correct and incorrect about it, and we can then go forward. So our request this morning would be also that the Court order that that be translated in a very expeditious manner, so that we can get on with preparing our trial brief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Jokic is also a soldier, and we do need his assistance in preparing the pre-trial brief. But I just wanted to bring to the Court's attention that under Rule 65 ter (F), there is no need to have the Defence pre-trial brief filed that early. If we have our Pre-Trial Conference the first week in April, then we may -- if we set a date for the first week in March, I think that would be sufficient under the Rule 65 ter (F), and just to ensure the rights of the accused that all these documents are translated, that there has been sufficient ability to communicate and confer with your client. I think pushing it to January 10th may be stretching the translation department, who -- I'm still not clear if it's the responsibility of the Prosecution or if it's the Registry's responsibility, under your order, to do the translations, but I ask that the Court give us a little extra time so that, once it's translated, we have time to discuss it and confer with our clients. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other contributions to this point, related to the Butler report? Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. With respect to the Butler report, I concur with Mr. Wilson's position. I think that it is very complex, it's very necessary. Again, I want to draw the Court's attention that, under the Prosecutor, the outstanding indictment for Mr. Blagojevic was back in 1998. They made a big deal about it, him somehow not being available to be arrested for some several years because they had to uncover his whereabouts. But it would seem to me that if they had an indictment, they should have been actively pursuing, through their military expert, preparing a report that would also cover the brigade level. Now, Mr. Blagojevic was arrested and we -- over a year ago. He's been in detention. We've had to wait for a very long time for Mr. Butler to prepare his report. And in my opinion, and I say this regrettably, it's totally inexcusable that we don't have it at this point in both languages, and it's inexcusable that it took so long for Mr. Butler to prepare his report, albeit he's very busy. My other concern is that we do -- we have noticed that there's a British general that is also going to be preparing some sort of a report. And I don't want to sound like Cassandra, but I dare say, I'm going to be back here arguing that I need that report as well translated. So perhaps the Court could factor that in as well. I don't know whether the Butler report can be prepared by December 10th, whether it can be translated, keeping in mind that there are also footnotes to these documents. Some of the documents may or may not be -- they may need to be translated, because they may be in English, although I think the majority of the documents that are referenced are in B/C/S, so that's not a problem. But nonetheless, we need it because also we need to cross-reference to make sure that the documents jibe in some way, that they're consistent, or where there are inconsistencies, so we can go through that. I don't particularly have a problem with the January 10th deadline. It does -- you know, puts us under the gun a little bit, because you also have the holiday season and what have you, and some may or may not have plans, especially if they have families. But if we were to get the report by December 10th, I'm willing to make a commitment that I'll have my pre-trial brief by January 10th. Barring that, it would be very difficult, Your Honour. I don't want to get it five days before. So I urge you, please, you know, put some heat on the Prosecution to get it done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary, because I have the impression all the parties do whatever they can in preparation of the case. May I ask Mr. McCloskey: Do you believe it's realistic to have the Butler report also translated until the 10th of December?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I asked for an estimate on when Butler's report can be fully translated, and the response I have is the end of January. Now, I say that -- I think we should also point out Mr. Butler's report -- the vast majority of it has already been written and is in B/C/S, from the Krstic trial. We're flattered that the Defence is so concerned about the rest of it, and we agree that they should see it and that it is important. It's largely due to incorporating new material in the report that is important and that the Defence should see. The new material is a result of material we believe hidden by the RS government that we had to get from a search warrant to the MUP. So it's not by any fault of the Prosecution that this report and the materials in it have come at the time they did, which we did meet your deadline of the report filing. Now, what Mr. Butler has done, he has taken several days, I believe, at this point, to help the Translation identify the new parts of the report so that they would not go through what happens, unfortunately, so many times here, repeating the same translation over again. So they are translating the key parts of it. And also, we have a particular translator that is familiar with the terminology, familiar with the situation, and she -- it is her responsibility to work on it, with others, and with her supervisors. It's not only her product, but we get a better product if we rely on that one expert translator for the bulk of the work, and that's where the end of January comes in. Now, if it gets divided up to others, perhaps Translations can get it sooner. But Translation, as you're well aware, as I'm sure counsel is, are working full out on many cases, and there are cases where translations and documents are a real problem. This is not one of them. But I would only -- to get it sooner than January, we would need to talk to the supervisors at Translations to see what they say about it. I would like to get this report to the Defence as soon as possible, for the reason they have stated, and we have been working full out to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. It was also my understanding that, to a great extent, the Butler report contains material already used in the Krstic case and was already translated. We face this problem nearly in each and every case, and normally we try to come to the conclusion that it might be possible that when Defence counsel and accused meet, they assist each other - I'm making reference to the fact that some parts are referenced in B/C/S - that they assist each other when discussing this report. On the other hand, knowing that when the Translation Unit is under inhuman stress, there might be some flaws in the interpretation, and this should be avoided, because especially this report, also I myself don't have any, as you must all know, experience in this area, I have to rely on the accurateness of the translation, and therefore there shouldn't be any undue time pressure imposed on the Translation Unit. And therefore, I would ask the Defence -- all Defence counsel to be prepared with a pre-trial brief, in general, the 10th of January, 2003, notwithstanding that when receiving the final Butler report, there may be an amendment to this pre-trial brief. I think this is a reasonable solution. Can you all agree with this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that we're trying very hard to negotiate and come up with a compromise on all this, but the fact is the new Butler report is the one that contains 90 per cent of the evidence relevant to this case, because they have now included the Zvornik Brigade. So it's very difficult for us to prepare a Defence pre-trial brief without having access to the translation of the new Butler report and the new evidence prior to that time. I think it might be duplicious [sic] if we file one brief and then have to file another, but I just want to bring it to your attention that the new Butler report is the one that's most relevant to the Defence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt I'm aware of this, and you may know that we ask the Prosecution to provide us with the same material that the Defence receives - no more, of course, but also no less - because we want to know the facts, we want to be prepared, and we are aware of the importance of the Butler report. But nevertheless, I think it is worthwhile, and it's possible to discuss, in part, the Butler report, due to the fact that the Defence teams are composed of counsel speaking both languages together and therefore can discuss the Butler report already now, in the general outlines, with their clients. I don't regard this as would be an impediment, to have the pre-trial brief prepared 10 January. And then, when receiving the translation in full, I would ask the Prosecution to tell us the exact date when this translation was sent to Defence counsel. And from this point in time, we would grant leave to amend, if need may be, one other month for such an amendment of the pre-trial brief. I think this is necessary, because we can't wait until the beginning of April with a Pre-Trial Conference. I want to avoid two extremely expensive and, in part, overlapping conferences. Under the Rules, we have to have the next Status Conference no later than 26 March 2003, and this should serve already as the Pre-Trial Conference in order to prepare. Maybe at that time we need even more than one day. I hope that it will be possible for the parties to proceed this way. And as stated, first of all, the pre-trial brief has to be translated, and this should be, and as ordered, no later than 10 December. But may I ask now the Prosecution once more, in relation to the -- I wouldn't call it complaints, but the observations by the Defence related to 66(A): What about your point of view regarding witness statements to be treated as documents or not documents? The reference to the Rutaganda, in all politeness, a rather fast decision taken at that point in time. Do you believe that at least some of the points raised by the Defence can be solved by the Prosecution and between the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe that I have -- and that we have solved them together. I don't see the problem that counsel have seen, and I'll explain why. The issue whether or not statements amount to documents under reciprocal discovery has been briefed by both sides. There's a policy of the OTP that they do not -- statements are not documents. And that material, as Mr. Karnavas said, is awaiting your decision, if need be, and we would welcome a decision, as would the Defence. But what we have done together, in order to avoid any problem, is we've agreed to provide the Defence with statements. And it's rather interesting -- Mr. Karnavas wants all these statements. We have endeavoured to give all parties all statements that we felt may be material, and Mr. Londrovic feels prejudiced by that very fact. What we're doing in order to meet our obligation under our agreement is providing the Defence, wherever possible, with searchable CDs of our basic collections, and the collection that has offended Mr. Londrovic is the collection of Muslim witness statements, that some of them may deal mostly with 1992, though I would suggest the bulk of them involve Srebrenica, but 1992 is, of course, also part of this indictment. So in order to err on the side of caution, we have provided, in CD electronic searchable format, all our Muslim witness statements that we felt we could provide under confidentiality agreement and -- to them, that -- aside from any statements that were not material or not relevant and that would get someone hurt if they were turned over. And that's what we've been doing. And we have been providing the vast majority of our file in order to avoid Rule 68 problems, in order to avoid discovery issues of this sort. Now, I personally in my own discretion have gone outside the Rules in order to deal with this problem head on so we wouldn't have such a problem. I view, I believe, the correct standard under reciprocal discovery is material what is material to the preparation of the defence. That is even broader than the term "relevant" as a legal term, and that is what I am viewing. Personally, I'm viewing this matter as something that may be material to the preparation of events. I view that broadly. I've also agreed to provide Serb witness statements, which is something the Defence have indicated a great interest in, for obvious reasons, and we are endeavouring and have provided them with almost all the Serb witness statements that we've had. And as I've told counsel, there are certain confidential material that we do not intend to use as evidence, and the turning over of that material may endanger the people that provided it, and the Rules make protection for those folks. But I don't know what other pockets Mr. Karnavas wants to reach into, but most of my pockets are open, and he's welcome to reach. But I don't really think we have a problem. I think naturally there's some concern that since he can't look in the closet, he's not sure, you know, what's there, but I think at some point we have to rely on the professionalism of other folks. And I'm not saying there won't be mistakes. This is a huge problem and there may be things that we miss or that trickle in. We're trying our best every day that that doesn't happen, but I don't know what else I can say on this. We've gone beyond the law, and we're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I understand that you leave the question open whether these witness statements have to be regarded as documents or not and under which Rule they fall, but taking the pragmatic approach and disclosing all the statements you regard as material. May I then ask the Defence whether, having heard this, they see a problem, because we are not here to resolve theoretical problems when already, from a practical point of view, solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, as you indicated, all material the Prosecution regards. Now, the Prosecutor, unless he has a mole in my Defence team or listening device, doesn't know what my defence is, doesn't know where I'm going, may not necessarily know what is or is not material. Now, as a professional Prosecutor, he has a pretty good understanding, but -- and that may be with respect to 95 per cent of my case. It is the 5 per cent that may -- that may not make the difference, however. In this case or some of the other cases, it is that 5 per cent difference that often, in this particular Tribunal, grows to be 10, 15, and 20 per cent. I think we have -- after so many years, we have a body of law and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a body of cases that suggests that more often than not, under Rule 115, cases are coming back because, lo and behold, the parties have learned that material existed in the possession of the Prosecution that should have been provided. Maybe at the time they didn't think so because they looked at it, they didn't think it to be material. We know that in the Krstic case, for example, that happens to be the case. They have admitted in fact that they haven't turned over certain material which they believed to fall under Rule 68. And material does fall, you know, between the cracks, you know, that may be turned over, but if you look at case after case after case, you see that there is a problem with disclosure. Now, each of us -- each of the Defence teams in this particular case has signed a confidentiality agreement with the Prosecution. We are all abiding by that. I haven't heard any complaints. Therefore, we are mandated not only by our agreement but also by, I think, our oath as officers of the court to abide by all of the Rules and to ensure that nobody's safety is compromised. I, frankly, cannot see the problem, you know, in the Prosecution not allowing us to see his entire file barring that which he feels is work product. And I would say, for the record, that notes that are generated in the field by investigators do not fall under that, you know, area of work product, because they may contain material which is material to my defence. And at least in adversarial proceedings, work notes, notes that are generated during an investigation, are discoverable. I'm not suggesting that those exist, but I'm just saying those are the sort of materials that I would like to see if it's available. And also with respect to statements. The Prosecutor says he turned over statements which he believes are material. Not "the statements" that he has. And that's my concern. And he's right, and he's absolutely right, and I think if he was here, he would be making the same argument. Since I'm not able to peek in the closet and actually roam around the closet and go through everything in it, I don't know what exists. And I don't want to be here three years or four years from now, making a Rule 115 argument because of material that was available. And he has and the Rules provide a safety mechanism and a safety valve, and that's you, Your Honour, and your colleagues. You can look at it in your private setting and then make the decision whether it is relevant, relevant in the sense that -- you know, also is it admissible at trial. And I agree with Mr. McCloskey that the term "material" is slightly broader, but again I want to re-emphasise that, given that we have a history of repeated failures and human failures. I'm not suggesting anything sinister, but failures nonetheless in case after case after case. There's absolutely no reason why we cannot have the entire file. If he feels that certain material should only be viewed by the Bench, I don't have a problem with that. At least we have a record of what is there. And I think coming back to your legal tradition, Your Honour, and in the continental system, you would be entitled to the entire file, all of it. You would look at it. And why is that? You certainly don't rely on the Prosecutor to tell you what is material for you to find the truth in the case. Well, the same thing here. I certainly don't want the Prosecutor telling me what he thinks is material in my preparation of my defence, because I may prepare my case slightly differently than he or his colleagues believe that to be. And I brief this issue I think quite well in my reply. I'm more than happy to expand on that. I went over the page limitation. I can produce a Law Review article on that, and I think it would come back to the same conclusion, and that is I need it all because all of it is material. And with all due deference to my colleague who represents Mr. Nikolic, even that material may at some point become relevant in this case, even though it dates back to 1992 versus 1995, if we're going to be hearing from the Prosecution, and I dare say it's likely that he's going to try to bring in incidents relating to 1992 and using that as part of -- because you see that in the indictment, and using that as part of the chain of events leading up to 1995, and therefore, that material obviously may become material. We don't know. Whether it becomes relevant at trial, that's for the trial Bench to decide, whether it's relevant, whether it's probative versus prejudicial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Before giving the floor to other Defence counsel, I have the impression that in fact we don't have before us the legal question whether these witness statements should be categorised as documents or not, but coming down to the ordinary question whether or not the material or relevant documents were disclosed in full as expected under Rule 66. And you made reference, as I did before, to the continental law system, but we have to obey to the Rules of this Tribunal, and there Rule 66, as well as Rule 68, to be disclosed later, they both rely on the professionalism of the Prosecution and that they do what they can, and no doubt it's extremely hard to find out among this I think what is 2 million or 3 million documents you have available in your database, to find out documents, and there might be a flaw. But I think when we work together, and this is not only true for this Status Conference but also for the trial in future, it's absolutely necessary that we can rely, vice versa, on each other's professionalism and working conscientiously. And I think none of the Defence counsel until now has disputed that in this case the Prosecution did whatever possible, even leaving aside this legal question whether witness statements have to be treated as documents or not. So may I ask, is there a feeling by any other Defence counsel that one of you would be prejudiced by the disclosure as it happened until now under Rule 66?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might. In light of the memorandum by the Prosecutor's office, which basically has a ruling contrary to the Rutaganda ruling in which statements are considered documents under 66(B), since the Prosecution has taken the opposite position, although we have a very good working relationship with the Prosecution, I do believe that they try their best to comply with discovery requests, I think that it's time that we have a ruling from this Court on whether this Court considers 66(B) to include witness statements or not just for the future, because in order for us to have a ruling, we can negotiate between the parties, we can work between the parties, but we have to know exactly the legal framework that we're working under. Therefore, I just re-urge this Court to issue a ruling on the September 15th motion that we filed with regard to the issue do witness statements fit under material that should be given to the Defence under Rule 66(B).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kirsch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KIRSCH
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. Just to clear up maybe a misunderstanding we had with what my learned counsel Mr. Londrovic said before. It is not that we don't want all the things. It was only irritating to us that we think that there must be more material we don't have. So we are just looking where we get this, and we are irritated because we think there is material in it which might prejudice our client. We have -- I have full trust that Mr. McCloskey does everything what's possible, and I don't think that he is doing intentionally something to prejudice our client, but it would be very much more -- it would be much more easier for us if we could say we have the entire file. Then we wouldn't have the feeling that maybe something, because we know that you, Your Honour, like to see the material given to the Defence, we would be much more comfortable if we could say you and we got all the materials. Then we don't have the differentiation between what is material in the eyes of Mr. McCloskey or in our eyes. So I would strongly support what Mr. Karnavas said before, and Ms. Sinatra. I think we are entitled to the whole file, given the structure of the indictment based on the joint criminal enterprise theory. This is another strong argument to be entitled to the whole file. So I would strongly ask you for this ruling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other submissions, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have nothing to add to our earlier comments. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. No doubt the Trial Chamber has then to rule on the remaining points, but I wonder what are the remaining points. First, to request all material. That's easy said but difficult done. The Judges themselves, we don't have access to the entire database of the Prosecution. Therefore, "all the material" de facto would mean access to all the documents available for the Prosecution because each document may have to a certain extent a context with our case, and it might touch upon -- I want to avoid in this context word "material" and "relevant", but there might be the same names or the same locations but in a totally different context. So I wonder how under the Rules the Trial Chamber should order to disclose all material. I think in case the Defence has the impression that concrete documents or witness statements were not provided, were not disclosed, then this would have been to demonstrate it in concreto. The second problem, it's extremely difficult to rule on an issue what, from a legal perspective, seems to be moot when the Prosecution already has decided to leave the question open whether this has to be disclosed as a document or as a statement, but leaving the question aside, disclosing all the statements they regard as material or relevant, and as I understood, notwithstanding that there might come in two or three other to be finally translated witness statements, they fulfilled their obligation, because we can't decide a legal question in a vacuum. So therefore, I wonder, what can be the outcome of such a decision in this concrete point in time. But I don't expect that there will be any other submissions by the parties at the moment. I only alerted the parties what might be the outcome of such a decision. I understand that there are no other problems related to 66. Let's now turn to Rule 68. May I once again first ask Mr. Karnavas. Rule 68. Do you have any problems related to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: None that I'm aware of at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But I would just want to say if you would rule in my favour on my 66, we would definitely never have any problems on the 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wilson, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: No problems at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SINATRA
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course we still believe that under Rule 68 that the best person to determine what is exculpatory evidence is the Defence, not the Prosecution. But also I have another motion on file - and I don't have a copy of it before me - having to do with the fact that it's very difficult to determine what is exculpatory and -- exculpatory evidence under Rule 68 when we only get a witness summary from the Prosecution. And there was a ruling recently in the Brdjanin case which states that we have a right to have the entire statement instead of just a witness summary to best -- to put the Defence in the best position to determine what is exculpatory and what isn't. I have the case in front of me, but I'm sure Your Honour is familiar with it, and I'd like to ask the Court to rule, number one, that we be given complete statements instead of witness summaries, in order to determine what is exculpatory. But number two, just recently I received a piece of exculpatory evidence, and it's only because I asked for this witness statement. And if I had not known about it, then I would not have been privy to this exculpatory evidence. I still believe that pursuant to Rule 66, if we get all the evidence, then we're the best ones to determine what is exculpatory and what isn't, and the only way to do that is by seeing the whole statement, not a summary that has been protracted by the -- protracted from the original statement by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Veselin Londrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of the accused Nikolic believes that the Prosecutor is fulfilling his obligations under Rule 68 fully and professionally, and at present, we have no complaints and no comments on the work of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then may I ask the Prosecution what about this problem mentioned by Ms. Sinatra, providing summaries instead of entire statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I do have a problem with Rule 68, and that's one of the reasons why I've personally taken the discretion to provide almost all of my file, because I think they are in the best position to figure out what that Statute means. And I'm not sure exactly what she's referring to. If it is a statement of Vinko Pandurevic, it may be that that's all we have. We don't always do question/answer statements. Sometimes we have third-party summaries of what someone said. And if that's the case, you have what we have. Other times, when Rule 68 may come from a protected witness or perhaps a Rule 70 source, we provide summaries in order not to identify that source, and I believe that's the best way to do it. And I don't believe we've had to do that yet in this case, or at least often, and I will try to explore our record to see if we have. But I do, in terms of protecting confidential witnesses, do need to have their best security in mind, and the rules under 66(C) and Rule 70 provide that -- me that right. And so in those cases, I would prefer to provide summaries. And again, I do that on my own discretion. There are -- there is still an issue whether or not Rule 68 trumps Rule 70 or Rule 70 trumps Rule 68. And again, that is not an issue I wish to litigate here at the trial level. And I will, as I see material that may be Rule 68, I will provide it to the Defence counsel. And in order to protect the identity of a witness or person, I would like to have the ability to summarise it in such a way as to protect that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I have the impression that here we come at the first time in this case to really agreed facts amongst the parties and the Judges as well, because no doubt it's for the Defence to decide which document or statement they regard as exculpatory in the sense of Rule 68.
